chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about a man: does anything cut off his prayer from what passes in front of him? He said: Nothing cuts off the prayer of a Muslim, but ward off what you can.

He said: And I asked him about a man who had a nosebleed, and his nosebleed did not stop until the time for prayer entered. He said: He should stuff his nose with something, then pray, and not prolong (the prayer) if he fears the blood will overtake him.
He said: And he said: When you turn your head in an obligatory prayer before completion, repeat the prayer if the turning is excessive; and if you have already performed the Tashahhud, do not repeat.
ai.seo_question: What breaks the validity of Islamic prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that minor distractions like passing objects do not invalidate the prayer, reflecting the Shia principle of ease (yusr) in worship, while providing a pragmatic solution for nosebleeds that prioritizes completing the obligatory act. The ruling on turning the head distinguishes between significant deviation (which requires re-prayer) and minor movement, emphasizing that intention and degree of distraction determine validity rather than rigid physical stillness. This hadith is foundational in Usul al-Fiqh for understanding the boundaries of nullifiers (mubtilat) versus mere detractors of concentration (khushu).
